title: The body as a boat
hookLine: a twelve-step skincare routine on one side, four hours of sleep and cold pizza on the other; Shantideva says: a boat
tomorrow: how much good can a single flash of anger burn?

lines: A BODY AS A RENTAL CAR.
cards: Scroll for a minute and you'll see two kinds of people. One has a skincare routine with a dozen steps, a mirror selfie after every workout, a body that's become a full-time project.
The other is running on four hours of sleep, cold pizza and a deadline, treating the body like a rental car they'll return someday. Both feel normal.
So, yesterday's question: is the body something to worship, or something to use? Shantideva's answer is neither, exactly. It's a boat.

teach.b: Chapter five holds two views of the body, and both are honest Buddhist voices. View one: don't make it an idol.
Shantideva asks the reader to look closely at the body, skin, flesh, bone, and to see that there's nothing in it worth clinging to as if it were the whole point.

Why guard it so jealously, he asks, when it will be left behind? The best case for this view: it frees you. A body that isn't an idol can age, scar and change without your whole self going down with it.
View two: don't wreck it. The same chapter says the body that carries the teaching shouldn't be harmed for some small reason. And elsewhere the poem calls this human life hard to find.
The best case here: a body you starve and exhaust can't help anyone, including you. Then Shantideva brings the two together in one picture.

teach.h: A SUPPORT FOR COMING AND GOING.
teach.b: Regard the body as a boat, he says, simply a support for coming and going, used for the good of beings.
A boat isn't worshipped. Nobody burns incense to the hull.
But nobody sails a boat with holes in it either. You patch it, you bail it out, and you take it somewhere that matters.

how: Buddhist teachers hold together two teachings on the body: reflecting on its impermanence so it isn't clung to, and valuing a human life as a rare chance to practice; monastic rules include care for health, food and medicine.

games.q: what does “the body as a boat” mean?
o: caring for the body and using it for good, not clinging
a body trained hard until it can carry heavy loads
an old belief that the body floats after you die

games.q: two views, one boat — tap the pairs.
p: don't make the body an idol
don't harm it for a small reason
a support for coming and going

s: Buddhism teaches that the body is bad and should be neglected
Shantideva warns against clinging to it and against harming it for small reasons.
Shantideva says to regard the body as a boat
a support for coming and going, used for the good of beings.

games.q: your friend is training for a race and runs through a painful injury because 'pain is weakness leaving.' in Shantideva's two views, which best case fits?
o: view one: the body isn't the point, so ignore the pain and push on.
view two: don't harm the boat for a small reason; rest it and sail later.
neither: the body should be pampered so it never feels pain at all.
games.why: not clinging to the body doesn't mean wrecking it. Shantideva says not to harm it for a small reason; a boat with holes sails nowhere.

practice: Take a glass of water, or anything plain to drink, and hold it a moment before you sip. Taste it slowly, feel it go down, and notice the body receiving something simple and good. That's patching the boat: no fuss, no neglect.

wordCard.voice: The body as a boat: Shantideva's way through. Not worshipped, not wrecked, but cared for and used to carry good across.

orig.note: Sanskrit: boat, ship (nau). Shantideva asks the reader to think of the body as a boat.

carryVoice: A line for the day: a boat, not an idol, patched and sailing. That's chapter five's watchfulness, wrapped up.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 5.60-5.70 (examining the body, nothing to cling to; regard the body as a boat, a support for coming and going, for the good of beings) and 5.86-5.87 (the body that serves the true dharma should not be harmed for a trivial reason)
Bodhicaryavatara 1.4 (this human life, with its freedoms, is very hard to find)
